lead: Heat is not all equally useful. Of the heat Q drawn from a body at temperature T, only a part can ever become work, because any engine must reject heat to the surroundings at T₀. That part is the available energy; the rest is the unavailable energy. This chapter fixes the surroundings (the dead state), finds both parts for a source at constant temperature and for a body that cools, and shows that heat transfer across a temperature difference always loses available energy.
prereq: You need: the Carnot efficiency 1 − T₀/T, the entropy change ΔS = ∫δQ/T of a reversible process, and T–s diagrams, all from the second law and entropy.

sections.h3: The dead state and the surroundings

blocks.text: The surroundings (the environment) are a very large body at temperature T₀ and pressure p₀, usually 25 °C (298 K) or 27 °C (300 K) and 1 atm. Their temperature does not change when they take or give heat.

A system is at the dead state when it is in full equilibrium with these surroundings: the same temperature T₀ and pressure p₀, at rest (no kinetic energy), at the reference height (no potential energy), and with no chemical difference from the surroundings. At the dead state no work can be drawn from the system, so every quantity in this unit is measured from that state.
Some syllabi call available energy "availability" and unavailable energy "anergy".

sections.h3: Heat from a source at constant temperature

blocks.text: Let a reservoir at absolute temperature T give heat Q. The most work we can get from Q comes from a reversible (Carnot) engine working between T and T₀. Its efficiency is 1 − T₀/T, so

blocks.where: AE is the available energy in kJ; Q is the heat given by the source in kJ; T and T₀ are absolute temperatures in K; ΔS = Q/T is the entropy the source gives up, in kJ/K.
UE is the unavailable energy in kJ: the heat that even the reversible engine must reject to the surroundings.

blocks.text: On a T–s diagram the heat Q is the area under the source line. The horizontal line T = T₀ cuts that area in two: the part above the line is AE, and the rectangle below it, of height T₀ and width ΔS, is UE. With T₀ = 300 K, half of the heat from a 600 K source is available; from a 1200 K source, three quarters.

sections.h3: Heat from a body that cools

blocks.text: A real hot body, such as exhaust gas or hot water, cools while it gives heat, so its temperature is not fixed. Split the heat into small parts δQ, each given at the body's present temperature T, and add the Carnot work of every part. The result keeps the same form, AE = Q − T₀ΔS, where ΔS is the entropy the body gives up:

blocks.where: m is the mass in kg; c is the specific heat in kJ/(kg·K); the body cools from T₁ to T₂, both in K; the heat given is Q = m·c·(T₁ − T₂) in kJ.

blocks.text: The most work is obtained when the body cools all the way to T₀; below T₀ it would have to take heat from the surroundings instead. Figure 4.1.1 draws this for the first worked example: 10 kg of water cooling from 360 K to 300 K. The sliver above the T₀ line is small, because warm water gives its heat close to T₀.

sections.h3: Loss of available energy in heat transfer

blocks.text: Let heat Q flow from a hot reservoir at T₁ to a colder body at T₂ (T₁ > T₂) across a finite temperature difference. The energy is the same Q on both sides, but its available part is not. The loss is
S<sub>gen</sub> = Q/T₂ − Q/T₁ is the entropy generated by the transfer, in kJ/K. Both temperatures are absolute.

The loss is always positive, because 1/T₂ is larger than 1/T₁. Energy is conserved, but its quality falls: heat that has dropped in temperature can give less work. This is why a boiler, where hot combustion gas heats water that boils at a far lower temperature, is the biggest loss of available energy in a steam plant.

examples.question: 10 kg of water at 360 K is used as a heat source. The surroundings are at 300 K. Take c = 4.18 kJ/(kg·K). Find the heat the water can give as it cools to the temperature of the surroundings, and how much of it is available and how much unavailable.
steps: Given: m = 10 kg, c = 4.18 kJ/(kg·K), T₁ = 360 K, T₂ = T₀ = 300 K.
Entropy given up by the water: ΔS = m·c·ln(T₁/T₀) = 41.8 × ln 1.2 = 41.8 × 0.18232 = 7.621 kJ/K.
Available energy: AE = Q − UE = 2508 − 2286.3 = 221.7 kJ.
Check: the water gives its heat at a mean temperature Q/ΔS = 2508/7.621 = 329.1 K, and a Carnot engine at that temperature gives 2508 × (1 − 300/329.1) = 221.7 kJ, the same answer.
examples.answer: Q = 2508 kJ, of which 221.7 kJ (about 8.8 %) is available and 2286.3 kJ is unavailable. Warm water stores a lot of energy but little work.

examples.question: A reservoir at 1000 K gives 1000 kJ of heat to a system held at 500 K. The surroundings are at 300 K. Find the available energy of the heat before and after the transfer, the loss of available energy, and the entropy generated.
steps: After the transfer, at 500 K: AE₂ = 1000 × (1 − 300/500) = 1000 × 0.4 = 400 kJ.
Loss of available energy: AE₁ − AE₂ = 700 − 400 = 300 kJ.
Entropy generated: S<sub>gen</sub> = Q/T₂ − Q/T₁ = 1000/500 − 1000/1000 = 2 − 1 = 1 kJ/K.
Check: T₀S<sub>gen</sub> = 300 × 1 = 300 kJ, the same loss.
examples.answer: The available energy falls from 700 kJ to 400 kJ, so 300 kJ is lost, equal to T₀S<sub>gen</sub> = 300 K × 1 kJ/K.

traps: Putting °C into 1 − T₀/T or into ln(T₁/T₂). Convert to kelvin first: 87 °C is about 360 K.
Using Q(1 − T₀/T) for a body that cools. Its temperature changes, so use AE = Q − T₀·m·c·ln(T₁/T₂).
Taking T₀ as the temperature of an engine's sink or of its cooling water. T₀ is the temperature of the surroundings given in the question, often 25 °C or 27 °C.
Writing the loss in a heat transfer as T₀Q(1/T₁ − 1/T₂). That is negative; the colder body's term 1/T₂ comes first.
Calling unavailable energy "destroyed energy". It is not destroyed; it is energy that must leave as heat at T₀.

quiz.a: A state in full equilibrium with the surroundings: temperature T₀, pressure p₀, at rest, at the reference height and chemically like the surroundings. No work can be drawn from a system there.

quiz.q: Write the available and unavailable energy of heat Q from a source at constant temperature T.
quiz.a: AE = Q(1 − T₀/T) and UE = Q·T₀/T = T₀ΔS, with T and T₀ in kelvin.

quiz.q: On a T–s diagram, which area is the available energy of heat supplied along a curve?
quiz.a: The area under the supply curve and above the line T = T₀. The rectangle T₀ × ΔS below that line is the unavailable energy.

quiz.q: Heat of 2000 kJ is drawn from a source at 800 K. The surroundings are at 300 K. Find AE and UE.
5 kg of oil with c = 2 kJ/(kg·K) cools from 400 K to the surroundings at 300 K. Find its available energy.
Heat of 500 kJ passes from a reservoir at 900 K to one at 450 K, with T₀ = 300 K. How much available energy is lost, and where should an engine take the heat?
quiz.a: Loss = 300 × 500 × (1/450 − 1/900) = 300 × 500 × 0.0011111 = 166.7 kJ (AE falls from 333.3 kJ to 166.7 kJ). The engine should take the heat at 900 K, before it is degraded.

beyond: Waste-heat recovery engineers rank streams by available energy, not by heat: a large flow of 60 °C cooling water can hold less work than a small flow of 400 °C exhaust gas. Chemical exergy extends the idea to fuels. Search next: waste-heat exergy, organic Rankine cycle, chemical exergy of fuels.
